strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: expensive high-resolution annotations and poor transfer between DIS and salient object detection datasets. A 139,981-image synthetic dataset could be a valuable resource.
Reports substantial improvements across multiple real-world benchmarks. In Table 2, synthetic training reduces HRSOD-TE MAE from 0.030 to 0.016 relative to the same architecture trained on DIS.

Table 4 provides a useful size-matched comparison against MaskFactory and DatasetDM using the same downstream architecture. S3OD provides substantially better cross-dataset transfer, supporting the usefulness of its generated data.

Includes component ablations, qualitative examples, efficiency measurements, and a manual audit of 1,000 synthetic masks. The paper explicitly distinguishes oracle mask selection from deployable predictions.
weaknesses: The central mask-generation pipeline is insufficiently specified. Section 4.1 describes learned projections and feature fusion, but does not explain the supervision, training data, or optimization used to train the mask decoder. It also omits how training examples acquire corresponding FLUX features and which diffusion timesteps are used. Consequently, the pipeline cannot be reproduced and the claims of eliminating teacher bottlenecks and training without real annotations cannot be assessed end to end.

The feedback protocol leaves a potentially serious evaluation issue unresolved. Section 4.2 explicitly uses a held-out 'test set' to update category sampling, without identifying that set or establishing separation from reported benchmarks. The reference masks used to compute augmentation-averaged IoU are also unclear. An independent validation protocol is necessary to establish that cross-dataset results are not influenced by benchmark feedback.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the proposed generation mechanism from stronger pretrained models and larger training sets. Table 6 lacks a DINO-v3-only labeling baseline, although DINO-v3 supplies most of the demonstrated performance. Comparisons against older diffusion-based methods also change the image generator. Matched FLUX-Krea images labeled by a strong conventional teacher, and existing SOD architectures trained on S3OD, would clarify the specific contribution.

The iterative-generation evidence is weak. Table 5 does not establish equal dataset sizes and training budgets across rounds, so additional data may explain the gains. Moreover, the claimed 3.6% and 5.3% F-measure improvements contradict the displayed changes: 0.879 to 0.881 on DIS and 0.855 to 0.860 on DUT-OMRON. Repeated runs and an equal-size random-sampling control are missing.

The training objective contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3.1 selects the minimum-IoU branch despite describing the best prediction, while Figure 2 instead describes selection by predicted IoU. The stated focal loss includes only foreground terms and is summed over pixels, leaving its intended implementation and scaling unclear. These discrepancies prevent an unambiguous understanding of the method.

The ambiguity claim exceeds the evidence. Better oracle best-of-three performance does not establish that alternative masks are valid human interpretations; it can also reflect prediction errors or diversity. There is no multi-annotator evaluation or direct assessment of alternative-mask validity. Table 7 shows only modest improvements from three branches and degradation with two, without uncertainty estimates.

Reproducibility and high-fidelity validation remain incomplete. Training schedules, optimizer settings, input resolutions, category construction, and dataset access details are missing. Boundary-specific metrics would better substantiate pixel-precise segmentation claims. The manual audit lacks a detailed assessment protocol, and the FID evaluation omits its real reference distribution and sample sizes. These gaps are substantial for a paper whose main contribution is a synthetic dataset and its generation procedure.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: obtaining diverse, accurately annotated training data for high-resolution salient object detection. The proposed 139,981-image dataset could be a useful resource.

Reports substantial cross-dataset improvements across several benchmarks. Table 2 includes same-architecture real-data baselines, and Table 4 compares synthetic datasets at matched sample counts, providing meaningful evidence that S3OD data improves transfer.

Includes architectural and feature ablations, a manual audit of 1,000 generated masks, and practical inference measurements. The ground-truth-selected multi-mask results are explicitly identified as oracle results rather than directly comparable predictions.
weaknesses: The central mask-generation method is insufficiently specified. Section 4.1 describes learned projections and feature fusion but does not explain the supervision, training data, or training procedure that teaches this generator to produce masks. Training of the separate filtering model is also unspecified. These omissions prevent reproduction and make the claims of eliminating teacher bottlenecks and requiring no real training data difficult to assess.

The adaptive-generation evaluation protocol is ambiguous. Section 4.2 explicitly uses a 'held-out test set' to adjust category sampling, without identifying that set or establishing separation from reported evaluation benchmarks. It is also unclear whether the feedback uses ground-truth IoU, predicted IoU, or transformation consistency. If benchmark test data guide generation, the claimed cross-dataset generalization would be compromised; the manuscript needs to resolve this.

The ablations do not adequately isolate the proposed contributions. Table 6 lacks a DINO-v3-only mask-generator baseline, although removing DINO-v3 causes by far the largest degradation. Table 5 lacks a clearly documented equal-size, equal-compute static-generation control, so additional data and adaptive sampling remain confounded. Training established competing architectures on S3OD would also strengthen the dataset contribution.

The training objective contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3.1 selects the 'best' branch using argmin IoU, which selects the worst match, while Figure 2 describes selection by highest predicted IoU. These differ from selection by highest actual IoU. The stated focal loss also omits the background-class term. These may be presentation errors, but the implemented algorithm cannot be determined reliably.

The ambiguity claim exceeds the evidence. Better oracle best-of-three performance does not establish that alternative masks represent valid human interpretations. There is no multiple-annotation evaluation or human assessment of alternative masks. Table 7 shows only a modest improvement from one to three masks, while two masks perform worse; uncertainty estimates and mask-selection calibration are absent.

Several quantitative statements are inconsistent with the tables. Section 5.5 claims iterative-generation F-measure gains of 3.6% on DIS and 5.3% on DUT-OMRON, whereas Table 5 changes from 0.879 to 0.881 and 0.855 to 0.860. Inception Scores also differ substantially between Tables 8 and 9 without a clear protocol explanation, and the FID reference distribution and sample counts are unspecified.

Reproducibility and high-fidelity validation remain incomplete: optimizer settings, training schedules, input resolutions, diffusion feature-extraction timesteps, and generation costs are missing. The manual audit lacks a detailed annotation protocol or boundary-error measurements, and the evaluation does not directly establish the claimed pixel-precise boundary quality.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck: obtaining diverse, precisely annotated data for high-resolution salient object detection. The 139,981-image dataset could be a valuable resource.

Reports substantial improvements across multiple benchmarks. In Table 2, synthetic training reduces DIS overall MAE from 0.049 to 0.039 relative to the same architecture trained on SOD data; fine-tuned results also outperform strong baselines on several benchmarks.
Table 4 provides a useful size-matched comparison against MaskFactory and DatasetDM using the same downstream model, supporting the synthetic dataset's generalization benefits.

Combining diffusion features, concept attention, and DINO-v3 representations is plausible, and the paper includes architecture ablations, qualitative examples, and a manual audit of 1,000 generated samples.
weaknesses: The central mask-generation procedure is insufficiently specified. Section 4.1 introduces learned projections, feature fusion, and a decoder without explaining the supervision, training data, or training procedure used to learn them. The separate filtering model's training is also unspecified. Consequently, the synthetic-only and teacher-bottleneck claims cannot be adequately assessed or reproduced.

The adaptive generation protocol raises an unresolved evaluation concern: Section 4.2 explicitly uses a 'held-out test set' to update category sampling, without identifying that set or establishing separation from reported benchmarks. It is also unclear whether the feedback uses ground-truth IoU, predicted IoU, or transformation consistency. Benchmark independence must be established.

Ablations do not adequately isolate the proposed contributions. Table 6 lacks a DINO-only generator baseline, while Table 7 shows that changing the backbone produces substantially larger gains than adding mask branches. Table 5 does not establish equal dataset size and training budget across rounds, leaving adaptive sampling confounded with additional data.

The ambiguity claims exceed the evidence. Better oracle best-of-three performance does not establish that alternatives are valid human interpretations. No multiple-annotator evaluation or diversity analysis is provided; the deployable three-mask improvement is modest, and two masks worsen performance in Table 7.

The training specification contains consequential inconsistencies: Section 3.1 selects the minimum-IoU mask despite describing the best match, whereas Figure 2 describes selection by highest predicted IoU. The stated focal loss also omits the background term. These require clarification to determine the implemented objective.

Several quantitative claims do not match their tables. Section 5.5 reports iterative-generation F-measure gains of 3.6% on DIS and 5.3% on DUT-OMRON, whereas Table 5 changes from 0.879 to 0.881 and 0.855 to 0.860. Reproducibility is further limited by missing optimization settings, image resolutions, diffusion feature-extraction timesteps, generation costs, and the reference distribution for FID.

strengths: The 139,981-image synthetic dataset addresses an important annotation bottleneck in high-resolution salient object detection. Combining diffusion features, concept attention, and DINO-v3 representations is a promising practical approach.

Evaluation spans DIS, high- and low-resolution SOD, and camouflaged object detection. Table 3 shows that synthetic training also benefits BiRefNet and MVANet, providing evidence of dataset utility beyond the proposed architecture.
The paper includes size-matched comparisons against MaskFactory and DatasetDM, architectural and loss ablations, and a manual audit of 1,000 synthetic masks.
Deployable, non-oracle predictions achieve competitive results. The manuscript appropriately distinguishes ground-truth-assisted mask selection from standard inference.
weaknesses: The central cross-dataset comparison does not control the full supervision pipeline. Section 4.1 trains the mask generator using DIS, HRSOD, UHRSD, and DUTS annotations, whereas several baselines receive only DIS or SOD training data. The student uses synthetic images, but its labels indirectly incorporate supervision from both domains. A baseline using the same pooled real annotations is needed before attributing the reported advantage to synthetic-data generalization.

The claimed removal of teacher bottlenecks is insufficiently demonstrated: mask generation still depends on a supervised segmentation decoder. Table 8 omits a DINO-v3-only labeler, and there is no controlled comparison using identical FLUX images labeled by a strong conventional teacher. Consequently, the benefit of the proposed multimodal labeling mechanism over ordinary pseudo-labeling remains unclear.

The iterative-generation ablation confounds adaptive sampling with increasing dataset size. A uniform-sampling control at the same final size is missing. Moreover, the claimed 3.6% and 5.3% F-measure improvements contradict Table 7, which reports changes from .879 to .881 and .855 to .860, respectively. The identity and independence of the 'held-out test set' used for generation feedback also need clarification.

Important implementation details are absent, particularly how FLUX features and concept maps are obtained for the real annotated images used to train the mask decoder, and which diffusion timesteps supply those features. Training resolutions, optimizer schedules, exact split usage, and dataset/code availability are also insufficiently specified for reproduction.

The training objective is internally inconsistent. Section 3.1 and Appendix G select the minimum IoU despite describing best-match training, while Figure 2 describes selection by predicted IoU rather than measured ground-truth IoU. The stated focal loss includes only foreground terms. These discrepancies leave the implemented training procedure uncertain.

Evidence for ambiguity modeling is limited. Table 9 shows a much larger improvement from changing the backbone than from adding prediction branches, and two branches degrade performance. Oracle gains establish candidate coverage, but do not establish that alternatives are valid human interpretations. Multiple annotations or a human evaluation, together with mask-ranking accuracy, would better support this claim.

Several ablation improvements are small and lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates. High-fidelity boundary claims are evaluated primarily through aggregate region metrics and qualitative examples, without dedicated boundary-quality measurements. Together with the uncontrolled comparisons above, this leaves the evidence below the acceptance threshold despite promising practical results.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful bottleneck: obtaining diverse, accurately annotated data for high-resolution salient object segmentation. A dataset of approximately 140,000 image–mask pairs could be a useful resource.

The reported improvements extend across architectures. Table 3 shows that training BiRefNet and MVANet on S3OD improves transfer performance, providing evidence that the dataset’s benefits are not restricted to the proposed model.

The evaluation covers DIS, several SOD benchmarks, and camouflaged object detection. Table 5 includes a size-matched comparison against MaskFactory and DatasetDM, and the appendix provides additional baselines, efficiency measurements, and a manual audit of 1,000 synthetic masks.

The non-oracle model achieves competitive results, including DIS overall MAE of 0.029 versus 0.035 for BiRefNet and MVANet. The paper explicitly acknowledges that ground-truth-based selection among multiple masks is an oracle evaluation.
weaknesses: The central cross-dataset generalization comparison does not adequately account for upstream supervision. Section 4.1 trains the synthetic-mask decoder using DIS-5K, HRSOD, UHRSD, and DUTS annotations, whereas comparison models in Table 2 receive only DIS or SOD data. Thus, the synthetic-only student indirectly benefits from supervision in both domains. This does not establish test-label leakage, but it weakens the claimed transfer advantage over single-domain baselines. A pooled-real-data baseline and generators trained exclusively on the source domain are needed.

The generation pipeline is insufficiently specified at its most consequential step. The paper explains extracting FLUX features during image generation but does not explain how corresponding features, concept tokens, and diffusion timesteps are obtained for real annotated images used to train the mask decoder. Section 4.2 also adapts generation using an unidentified 'held-out test set'; its relationship to the reported evaluation sets must be clarified to establish an independent test protocol.

The evidence does not isolate the proposed multimodal labeling contribution from stronger pretrained components. Table 8 lacks a DINO-v3-only labeling baseline, despite DINO-v3 accounting for much of the performance. A particularly important missing comparison is conventional pseudo-labeling of the same FLUX-Krea images using an equally supervised DINO-v3 teacher. Comparisons with older Stable Diffusion-based datasets cannot establish that multimodal feature fusion eliminates teacher bottlenecks.

The iterative-generation ablation confounds adaptive sampling with increasing dataset size. There is no uniform-sampling control at the same final size and training budget. Moreover, the claimed 3.6% and 5.3% F-measure gains are inconsistent with Table 7: DIS increases from 0.879 to 0.881, and DUT-OMRON from 0.855 to 0.860. These small changes also lack uncertainty estimates.

The ambiguity claim exceeds the evidence. Better oracle selection against one annotation does not demonstrate that alternative predictions are valid interpretations. Table 9 shows a modest improvement from one to three masks and degradation with two; Table 15 shows nearly unchanged segmentation performance even without auxiliary regularization. Multiple human annotations or an assessment of alternative-mask validity would provide stronger support.

The training objective contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3.1 and Appendix G define the best branch using argmin IoU, which selects the worst overlap, while Figure 2 describes selection by highest predicted IoU rather than highest ground-truth IoU. The stated focal loss also omits the background term. These may be presentation errors, but the implemented objective cannot be determined reliably from the manuscript.

Reproducibility and high-fidelity validation remain incomplete. Optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, batch sizes, training and inference resolutions, and diffusion-feature extraction details are not adequately documented. The manual mask audit is useful, but lacks a precise assessment protocol, and the evaluation contains no dedicated boundary-quality metric despite emphasizing pixel-precise segmentation. Overall, the promising empirical results do not resolve the supervision, attribution, and reproducibility issues sufficiently for acceptance.

strengths: Addresses an important annotation bottleneck with a substantial dataset of 139,981 synthetic image–mask pairs and a plausible combination of diffusion features, concept attention, and DINO-v3 representations.

Evaluation spans DIS, several SOD benchmarks, and camouflaged object detection. Table 3 shows that S3OD also improves BiRefNet and MVANet, providing useful evidence that the dataset benefits architectures beyond the proposed model.
Includes equal-size comparisons against alternative synthetic datasets, real-data-only model baselines, component ablations, and a manual audit of 1,000 generated masks.
Reports competitive results using predicted mask selection and explicitly distinguishes ground-truth-assisted oracle results from deployable performance.
weaknesses: The central cross-dataset comparison does not control for supervision available to the full pipeline. Section 4.1 trains the mask generator using DIS, HRSOD, UHRSD, and DUTS annotations, whereas cross-task baselines use only DIS or SOD. Thus, synthetic-only student training still transfers supervision from both domains. A baseline trained on the same combined real datasets, plus matched pseudo-labeling controls, is needed to substantiate the claimed generalization advantage.

Critical implementation details are missing: how FLUX features are obtained for annotated real images when training the mask generator, which diffusion timesteps are used, and the optimization settings and image resolutions. Section 4.2 also uses an unspecified 'held-out test set' to guide generation. Its identity and separation from final benchmarks must be established; the current description leaves possible test-distribution adaptation unresolved.

The training objective is internally inconsistent. Section 3.1 and Appendix G select the minimum IoU despite describing best-match selection, while Figure 2 specifies the highest predicted IoU rather than ground-truth IoU. The stated focal loss omits the background term. These may be writing errors, but they leave materially different training algorithms compatible with the description.

Ablations do not sufficiently isolate the proposed mechanisms. Table 7 does not establish a fixed-size, fixed-compute comparison between adaptive and uniform generation. Table 8 lacks a DINO-only labeling baseline. Table 9 shows that replacing Swin-B with DINO-v3 produces a substantially larger improvement than adding multiple masks, making stronger controls especially important.

The ambiguity claim exceeds the evidence. Oracle best-of-three improvement does not establish that alternative masks are valid human interpretations. There is no multi-annotator evaluation, and Table 15 shows little segmentation benefit from preventing branch collapse. Human validity judgments and mask-selection calibration would strengthen this contribution.

Several claims overstate the reported results. Section 5.6 claims 3.6% and 5.3% F-measure gains from iteration, whereas Table 7 changes from .879 to .881 and .855 to .860. The blanket DIS state-of-the-art claim also requires qualification: Table 13 reports essentially tied aggregate performance with DIS-SAM. Small ablation gains lack uncertainty estimates.
